decisions.title: Fundraising at meal-service events (ethics)
decisions.reason_note: Fundraising approach affects charity's ethical standards and donor interaction policies.
decisions.recommendation:
Adopt passive QR code and lockbox only at meal-service events, with no direct asks of recipients. This protects the dignity of people you serve and avoids any perception of coercion or transactional charity, which is critical to your ethical standards and long-term trust. The tradeoff is you forgo potentially higher conversion from direct verbal asks, but the reputational and mission risk of asking recipients to donate while receiving aid is too high. The Flag Football event (Aug 8) already has vendor conflict issues (two vendors approached to sell at event and share proceeds, creating potential conflict with food sponsors), showing the complexity of mixing fundraising and service. Passive methods let recipients engage on their terms without pressure. First step: Steel drafts a one-page policy (passive QR and lockbox only, no direct asks, applies to all meal-service events) and circulates to Suhaib and Alexis for review by end of week. trainings.title: Module 1: Orientation, why this package exists
trainings.description:
Goal: understand the context and the problems this strategy package solves.

Welfare Avenue is a Montreal hunger relief NPO founded in 2020. As we grew, marketing was a recurring weak spot. MG&Co Consulting analyzed our organization and built a package to fix three connected problems: (1) Refined marketing plan: campaigns lacked a clear strategy, leading to insufficient donations. (2) Social media: disorganized content, inconsistent or late posts, no measurement. (3) Website: unstructured, weakening our brand image and donor credibility.

The package addresses all three with a target market definition, a social media channel strategy, a content template and calendar, a donor journey map, website and SEO recommendations, and a roles and communication model (RACI).

Key takeaway: hunger relief NPOs compete with hundreds of nonprofits for the same donors, which makes a clear, consistent, measurable marketing strategy essential, not optional.

Done when: you can name the 3 problems and explain why a deliberate marketing strategy matters for a small charity like ours.

trainings.title: Module 2: our target market, Gen Z and millennials
trainings.description:
Goal: know who we market to and why every content decision flows from this.

Because Welfare Avenue is small with an unestablished reputation, the package targets Gen Z and Millennials. Three reasons: (1) Blind trust: younger generations are more likely to trust and donate to smaller, lesser known charities (56% of Gen Z prefer giving to lesser known causes). (2) Social justice orientation: they care most about supporting marginalized communities and social causes. (3) Social sharing: they are highly active on social media and publicly promote causes they support, driving organic growth.

What this audience wants from content: Educational (about 50% research a cause thoroughly before donating). Shareable (42%+ share or promote causes on social media). Impact and transparency (they want to see exactly where donations go). Real and human (they distrust traditional ad tactics and trust authentic, personal content). Short and visual (attention spans of about 8s for Gen Z and 12s for Millennials, so video and image content wins).

Done when: you can name the target market, the 3 reasons we chose it, and the 5 content traits they respond to.

trainings.title: Module 3: social media strategy, channels and frequency
trainings.description:
Goal: understand which channels we focus on, why, and how often we post.

The old problem: we were present on almost every platform (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, YouTube, LinkedIn, TikTok) but posted rarely and inconsistently, often just 1 to 2 posts a month with no tracking.

The strategy: fewer channels, posted more consistently, aimed at donations. Given our limited student run resources, concentrate on four channels matched to our target market: Instagram (strong with the 18 to 35 core audience, 3 per week). LinkedIn (donors over index here; LinkedIn members are 56% more likely to donate than the average user; 3 per week). TikTok (our existing strength and the best platform to reach Gen Z; shift toward donation focused posts; 1 to 2 per week). YouTube (89% of Gen Z and 86% of Millennials watch weekly; good for deeper video; 1 per 3 months).

Principle: prioritize platforms with easy in app donation features, and keep frequency realistic for a volunteer team.

Done when: you can list the 4 priority channels, why each was chosen, and the target frequency for each.

trainings.title: Module 4: content template and content calendar
trainings.description:
Goal: understand the structure that makes every post purposeful and measurable.

The old problem: content was made ad hoc with no schedule, no target market focus, and no way to measure what worked.

The fix: a monthly content calendar where every post is planned against four elements. (1) Content category: a clear purpose or theme behind the post. (2) Media type: vary and label it (video vs image) so we can analyze which formats perform. (3) Clearly defined goal: each post serves a specific marketing goal; reviewing goals monthly confirms coverage. (4) CTA plus tracking link: every post includes a call to action and a tracking link so we can measure performance and impact.

Content ideas that fit our audience: infographics that educate, testimonials that show impact, hashtags that encourage sharing, donation driving videos, live event coverage, "where your donation goes" posts, behind the scenes and vlog content. Treat every event as an opportunity to film content.

Done when: you can list the 4 elements every planned post must have and explain why tracking links matter.

trainings.title: Module 5: the donor journey map
trainings.description:
Goal: understand how we turn first time viewers into repeat donors and advocates.

A Donor Journey Map (DJM) is a blueprint of how a donor interacts with us at each stage of engagement. The goal is donor retention and loyalty: more donations, repeat donors, and advocates.

The 4 stages: (1) Awareness: the person discovers Welfare Avenue (searching online, hearing from friends). (2) Consideration: they weigh whether we are worth donating to (watching our videos, seeing volunteers in action). (3) Decision: they donate (reading the donation page, choosing an amount). (4) Evangelize: they spread the word and promote us to others.

Customize per event: each major event (for example the Concordia Shuffle) gets its own DJM tailored to season, economic outlook, and audience.

Supplementary pieces that build loyalty: an Impact Statement (shows the difference donations make), the Annual Report (transparency on outcomes), and a Donation Survey (post donation questions to inform data driven decisions).

Done when: you can name the 4 stages in order and the 3 supplementary pieces that boost retention.

trainings.title: Our eight charitable activities
trainings.description: What we are registered to do, how each activity works in practice, and how to talk about it.

body.summary: The eight activities we described to the CRA when we applied for charitable status, what each one looks like in practice, and how to talk about our work.

blocks.text: When Welfare Avenue applied for charitable status, we described our work to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) as eight charitable activities. They are the backbone of everything we do: every serving, drive, workshop and partnership should trace back to at least one of them.
Our charitable purposes are the **relief of poverty** and the **advancement of education**. The eight activities are how we carry out those purposes, day to day.

Welfare Avenue is a youth-powered non-profit dedicated to fighting food insecurity and poverty through direct community action, delivering meals and essential support directly to people where they are.

blocks.note: From our 2026 brand guide and recent grant applications.

blocks.text: Tap an activity to open it. Each one has a purpose, the way we carry it out, and the teams involved.

items.sum: Building relationships with organizations, businesses and schools that share our mission, so we reach more people and pool resources.
how: Find organizations working on poverty, food security and inclusion, and learn about their impact.
Reach out, meet, and present our mission and current activities.
Write tailored partnership and sponsorship proposals with clear roles and shared projects.
Run the joint projects, then review the results together and adjust.
items.teams: Outreach finds and grows partners and sponsors, Marketing promotes, Operations runs the volunteer base and equipment, Finance tracks sponsorship and campaign money, and the executive team makes sure every partnership fits the mission.
items.extra: As a youth-powered organization, outreach also builds our volunteer base through schools, student associations and clubs.

items.sum: Relieving poverty by getting clothing, hygiene products and other essentials to people who need them, and connecting them with services.
how: Run donation drives with supermarkets, schools, colleges and companies.
Sort, store and distribute what comes in, with volunteers at every step.
Connect people with mental health, employment, housing and shelter resources through our network.
Gather feedback after each drive to make the next one better.
items.teams: Operations runs collection and distribution, Outreach brings in organizations and students, Marketing invites the community to contribute, and Finance tracks what we spend.

items.sum: Addressing food insecurity with free meals at our Sunday servings.
how: Fundraise for food and receive food donations.
Plan meals with Canada's Food Guide in mind: fresh, balanced and mostly plant-based.
Coordinate volunteer cooks, drivers and servers through the volunteering manager.
Serve with care: safely, respectfully and on time.
items.teams: Operations plans each serving, the recipes and the food, Finance tracks food spending and budgets, Marketing raises awareness of food insecurity, and Outreach finds funding for meals.

items.sum: Addressing isolation by making our servings and events places where people feel welcome and connected.
how: Organize free community events, indoors and outdoors, where everyone can take part.
Put the proceeds of paid events back into food, hygiene supplies and clothing.
Talk with the people we serve, one on one and in groups, to understand their needs and build real connection.
Help young people understand homelessness and reduce stigma.
items.teams: Operations makes each serving a place for real connection, Outreach and Marketing raise awareness of isolation, and Finance keeps money available for community events.

items.sum: Helping people meet their basic needs by knowing what support exists and how to reach it.
how: Make space for open conversation at servings to learn what people need, including dietary needs and preferences.
Bring in information from partner organizations on mental health, shelters, housing and employment training.
Turn it into clear infographics, factsheets and brochures that we share at servings.
items.teams: Operations makes sure people know where we will be and what is available, Marketing shows why access matters, and Outreach shares what people tell us they need.

items.sum: Engaging students and young people to take action on poverty and homelessness.
how: Network at schools such as McGill, Concordia, Dawson and Vanier.
Run campus events like bake sales and student gatherings to raise awareness, volunteers and donations.
Offer volunteer roles and run workshops that encourage civic engagement.
items.teams: Outreach works with schools and clubs, Operations sets new student volunteers up, and Marketing reaches students online.

items.sum: Joining forces with non-profits and charities on the issues that affect the people we serve.
how: Network with local organizations, charities and community workers.
Take part in advisory work on poverty, such as Campaign 2000 advisory meetings.
Attend events that highlight these issues, such as Disability Without Poverty and Dignity for All.
items.teams: Outreach connects with other charities, Operations runs joint volunteer events, and Marketing supports partners online.

items.t: A voice for the people we serve
items.sum: Working with people who share our concern, and bringing the lived experience of the people we serve into the conversation.
how: Attend forums and conferences on poverty and homelessness in Canada.
Listen closely through conversations and feedback surveys, and learn the barriers people face.
Use what we learn to shape our services and to raise awareness on social media.
items.teams: Outreach attends forums and conferences, Operations gathers feedback at servings, Marketing amplifies the voices of the people we serve, and the executive team keeps everyone coordinated.

blocks.text: Team names are as written in our submission. They map onto today's departments on the Hub.
Our 2026 brand guide describes the same work as four pillars. Here is how the eight activities feed them.

items.d: Consistent, well-coordinated food distribution, using the meal as a trust-building first step toward long-term reintegration.
Seasonal clothing, hygiene essentials and basic amenities, always offered with respect and solidarity.
Pop-ups, creative arts and recreational sports that break down barriers and build belonging.
Bridging street-level trust with housing, mental health and employment networks across our partners.

blocks.t: And the energy behind all four
blocks.text: Activities 6 and 8 are why we call ourselves youth-powered: young leaders mobilizing their communities, and a voice for the people we serve.
Our submission names **Place Émilie-Gamelin** (1500 rue Berri, by Berri-UQAM) as our main serving location, with a storage unit in Parc-Extension for the tents, tables and serving equipment.
Schools and campuses host much of our outreach, youth and education work: LaurenHill Academy, Vanier College, McGill, Dawson and Concordia.
Today we work in Montreal and Toronto, in parks, shelters and other community spaces.
The volunteering manager has the details of the next serving: date, place, roster and checklist. Take its page tour to see how it works.

chapters.t: Who we serve, and how we say it

blocks.text: We serve people experiencing homelessness or housing instability, low-income individuals and families, and anyone facing food insecurity. Support is based on need: people self-identify, or a partner organization refers them.
The words we use matter. If we call it the wrong word, someone reading gets the wrong image of what we do.

items: The people we serve, community, support
Support, dignity, connection, safety
Food as a starting point, refer, reintegrate
Youth-powered, professional, a movement
Collaborate, ecosystem, partnership
The homeless, beneficiaries, people in need
Pity, saving people, feeling sorry
Feed people, hand out food
Student club, just volunteers, a small project
We do everything, we're the only ones

blocks.text: Formal filings, like our CRA forms, use the word beneficiaries because it is the legal term. Everywhere else, we say the people we serve.
Advancing education is part of our charitable purpose, not an extra. We help our community understand food insecurity, isolation and access to resources, and invite them to act.

items: Workshops and presentations in schools, from LaurenHill Academy to Concordia.
Conferences such as Apathy is Boring, and Force Avenir, where we were selected in the Mutual Aid, Peace and Justice category.
Research and knowledge sharing: infographics, factsheets and information letters.
Social media that shows homelessness is about belonging and dignity, not only basic necessities.
Recruiting people who care about their community, and helping them grow professionally.

items.t: Tie your work to an activity
items.d: When you plan an event, a post or a partnership, know which activity it serves. It makes reports, grant applications and our annual return stronger.
If an idea does not clearly fit one of the eight activities or our purposes, check with the executive team before committing time or money.
Say the people we serve, and lead with dignity.
Log servings, volunteers and outcomes in the Hub so the numbers are ready when a funder or the CRA asks.

blocks.d: Our 8 Charitable Activities, the training copy of our submission to the CRA Charities Directorate.

questions.q: What are our two charitable purposes?
a: Relief of poverty and advancement of education
questions.why: Everything we do serves the relief of poverty and the advancement of education.

questions.q: Our Sunday servings mainly carry out which activity?
questions.why: Free, healthy meals address food insecurity. Servings touch other activities too, like community and belonging.

a: With Canada's Food Guide in mind: fresh, balanced and mostly plant-based
questions.why: Healthy meals are part of dignity: fresh ingredients, balanced and mostly plant-based.

questions.q: Which activity is about making servings and events places of belonging?
questions.why: Isolation is as real as hunger. Activity 4 is about welcome, conversation and connection.

questions.q: How do we refer to the people who come to our servings?
questions.why: We lead with the person, not their circumstance. Beneficiary is only the legal term in formal filings.

questions.q: You have an idea for a project that does not clearly fit any of the eight activities. What do you do?
a: Check with the executive team before committing time or money
questions.why: Our resources must go to our charitable purposes. A quick check keeps us compliant and often sharpens the idea.

trainings.title: Our partners and how we work with them
trainings.description: Partners, sponsors and collaborators, who we work with today, and how a partnership comes together.

body.summary: Why we partner, the difference between partners, sponsors and collaborators, who we work with today, and how a partnership comes together.

blocks.text: Welfare Avenue does not try to do everything itself. We complement the services that already exist and connect people with the right support. Partners make that possible.
Collaboration is the default. Until we build a larger audience, most events run with a partner org that shares the planning load.

items.d: Combining strengths, resources and expertise lets us reach more people, more effectively.
Programs shaped with partners reflect the communities we serve.
Co-created programs draw on shared knowledge and experience.
Kitchens, halls, equipment and networks, without duplicating effort.
Joint communication amplifies both missions.

blocks.text: Three words, three different relationships. Using the right one keeps our records, reports and thank-yous accurate.

items.d: An organization we work with toward a shared goal, through joint programs or initiatives. Formalized in writing: an MOU or a project agreement.

trainings.title: SOP: Flag Football tournament
trainings.description: How we run the summer flag football tournament with the Montreal Flag Football League: the partner, registration, sponsors, the day and the wrap-up.

body.intro: Our summer tournament with the Montreal Flag Football League (MFL). Teams register and pay a fee, the league runs the games, and we run everything around them: registration, sponsors, the booth, drinks, the raffle and the thank-yous. Two editions so far, both at Le Ber Park in Pointe-Saint-Charles. The league is what fills the fields, so the relationship with Terry comes first.
glance: A Saturday in August or early September (2025: September 6, from 2pm; 2026: August 8, 10am to 4pm)
Le Ber Park fields. Terry already rents them on Saturdays, so they cost us nothing. Backup: the Concordia Dome.
Montreal Flag Football League (Terry Babalis): the fields, schedule and divisions, referees, rules and the league mailing list (about 1,000 players)
About 5 months (the 2026 kickoff with Terry was March 26)
editions: 13 teams and 78 players across Competitive, Intermediate and Beginner, and over $2,800 raised (about $2,400 through Keela and about $400 on site). Guru (drinks), DOSE (ginger shots) and Lush (raffle prizes) gave in kind, and La Licorne de Feu sold food. Amanda led it, Jemeela ran the league relationship and registration, Rami brought the drinks and the student clubs, Alexis ran donations, and Ian and the marketing team made the content.

Our first edition with the league: about 12 teams, 6v6, from 2pm. Sportira gave winner jerseys and discount certificates and Athlon ran an activity station; food came from Costco and a bake sale. The event overview reports $2,500+ raised. Jemeela and Lina coordinated with Aksel, Daniela handled finance, Steel the sponsor asks, and Ian and Robert the posters and email.
An indoor tournament with a different league (Flag Plus).
roles: The plan, the sponsorship package and asks, the raffle, the budget, day-of setup and the post-mortem
Meetings with Terry, the Keela registration form, the registration sheet, vendors
In-kind asks (drinks, snacks, prizes) and student clubs
Raffle prizes, the donation table (Square and receipts), donor follow-up and the thank-you email
Interviews and reels, newsletters, LinkedIn, league and club reposts, day-of photos and video
The league relationship and the storage unit
Fields, schedule and divisions, referees and equipment, rules, the league mailing list

phases.title: Lock the partner and the date
steps: Meet Terry: the date, the fields, the divisions, what the league provides (referees, equipment) and what we provide.
Pick a date away from the between-season gap, when many players are on vacation.
Set the goal and a quota of teams from our own network (for example 5).
Agree in writing on any food vendor and their share of sales, and on who sells what.
Open the event budget (2026 planned about $330 in costs).

phases.title: Forms and the sponsor package
steps: One bilingual Keela registration form: team name, division, captain, and every player's email. Turn on the confirmation email.
Test the payment link end to end before it goes out.
Write the sponsorship package and start the sponsor tracker.
Plan the content calendar with Marketing: interviews, promo reels, newsletters.

phases.title: Sponsors and content
steps: Start the sponsor asks wide and early: in 2026, more than 40 asks brought 3 in-kind yeses. In-kind is easier to get than cash.
Film the interviews (the league, players).
Send a save-the-date to past teams, the league list, student clubs and corporate friends.

phases.title: Open registration
steps: Open registration with the first promo post and a newsletter.
Ask Terry to email the league list: it brings most of the teams.
Pitch student clubs and companies with a one-pager, and follow up by phone.
Ask staff, volunteers and partners to enter a team.

phases.title: Push sign-ups, lock suppliers
steps: Check registrations every week and share the count with Terry.
Confirm the food vendor and the drinks; file the in-kind forms that need lead time (DOSE needs about two weeks).
Plan the raffle and the donation table.
Keep registration open into the last week (in 2025, 4 to 8 teams signed up in the final days), and publish the format early.

phases.title: Close, schedule, pack
steps: Close registration and send Terry the sheet of paid teams; the league builds the schedule.
Buy drinks and supplies, print the QR donation flyers and signs.
Confirm who does setup, the booth, the raffle and photos.
Plan for heat: water, shade, sunscreen.

phases.title: Thank, reconcile, learn
steps: Thank the players, sponsors and the league within a week.
Reconcile the money (Keela, Square, cash, cheques, costs, the vendor's share) and record the result on the events calendar.
Post the recap content.
Hold the post-mortem, with the league too, and update this SOP.

dayof: 9am: pick up the tent, 2 tables and the cooler from the storage unit (a sedan fits 2 tables). 9:30am: on site.
Set up the booth: tent, tables, drinks, the raffle table, the Square reader, QR donation flyers, receipts and a speaker.
The 2026 format: 6v6 on 3 fields, at least 4 games per team, 20-minute halves in 30-minute slots, finals by division at 3:30pm.
Staff the booth all day: talk to players about the people we serve and what is next (Rally Paper, the donor program).
Do not sell what the food vendor sells.
Photos and video for the recap; announce the winners.
Pack up and return everything to the storage unit.
money: Income: team fees ($180), free agents ($30), on-site donations and the raffle, and sponsors.
2026: about $2,400 through Keela and about $400 on site, over $2,800 before costs. The costs and the vendor's share were not recorded: record them next time.
2025: the event overview reports $2,500+; the Costco run was about $356.
The 2026 plan assumed 40 teams ($7,200 in fees). Terry expects 15 to 20 league teams and says the fields handle 30 well, so our own network has to bring the rest.
lessons: The league fills the fields: nearly every team came through the league, so plan the numbers with Terry.
Bring our own teams: set a quota and ask staff, volunteers, partners and companies early.
Send the save-the-date months ahead.
Close registration later, and share the schedule early.
One bilingual form, and capture every player's email so we can thank them and invite them back.
Put any vendor's share in writing, and do not sell the same products side by side.
Staff the booth to talk to players, not just to take payments.
Agree who does what between Fundraising and Operations for setup.
Kids' activities only with pre-registration (none came in 2025).
Thank everyone within a week.
confirm: The 2025 team count and total (sources say 12 or 13 teams and $2,100 to $3,000).
The 2026 costs, the vendor's share and the net.
Waivers, insurance and first aid do not appear in past plans: confirm with the league what covers the players.

trainings.title: SOP: Rally Paper (playing as a charity team)
trainings.description: How we field a team in Rally Paper Montreal, the 36-hour student challenge where charity teams play for prize money: recruiting, squads, shifts and the weekend.

body.intro: Rally Paper Montreal is a 36-hour challenge run by an outside organizing team (Rayan is the founder). A few charities each field a team, and the prize money goes to the winning teams' charities. We do not run the event: we recruit, organize and lead our team. Headcount decides the placing, so this SOP is about getting enough people, early, into the right squads.
glance: A weekend in late September, Saturday 8am to Sunday afternoon (2025: September 27 and 28; 2026: September 19 and 20)
Rally Paper Montreal (Rayan). JMCC sends delegates, who count their shifts toward their volunteer hours.
$7,000 for first, $2,000 for second, $1,000 for third, and $500 to the charity of the MVP
3rd in 2025 ($1,000, received October 15, 2025); reportedly 3rd again in 2026 (to confirm)
About 3 months, from the organizer briefing in June or July
Small: flyers and printing. The organizer supplies shirts and cars.
format: A booklet drops every 2 hours from 8am Saturday; the last one drops at 2pm Sunday. Late submissions are disqualified.
Squads: Online, Treasure hunt, Logic and trivia, Quest, and Challengers (physical). In 2026 quest and trivia shared a slot, so we ran four squads.
Trivia in 2026: 6 booklets of 70 weighted questions, 2 hours to return each Excel file, no AI tools.

Physical crews are gender-balanced (2025: 12 people, 6 and 6, with waivers and the list sent in advance; 2026: up to 10, plus smaller crews of 3 to 5). The schedule comes early and the exact place 2 hours before each challenge.
Pre-challenge videos count: in 2026 the team intro video was judged on likes, comments and shares.
Posts go on an Instagram account the organizer lends us (ours was @rally.avenue). Every video opens with the Rally Paper banner, and sponsor challenges are mandatory and worth triple.
editions: Base camp in the JMSB building, about 75 people on the roster and about 40 JMCC sign-ups; reportedly 3rd again. Amanda managed the project, Steel led outreach and media and co-led the physical squad with Ryan (JMCC VP Charity), Alexis and Ian co-led online, Jemeela, Tate and Ibrahim led quest and trivia, Ahmed and Marina led the treasure hunt, and Ian and Kahkashan made the intro video.

Our first edition: 3rd place and $1,000 for Welfare Avenue, and a challenge that put Steel on CTV News. About 40 active players. Steel led the team and the physical squad, Ian led online, Mohamed led quest and trivia, Amanda (then with JMCC) brought the delegates, Jemeela moved sign-ups into WhatsApp, and Soraya ran the newsletters and the results email.
roles: The plan, the roster, the leads meeting and the post-mortem
Two per squad (one for Saturday, one for Sunday): online, treasure hunt, trivia and quest, physical
Student clubs, JMCC delegations, tabling and the sign-up form
The pre-challenge videos, the lent Instagram account and weekend content
Food and drinks for base camp, and logos in time for the shirts
Track and verify the hours of JMCC delegates

phases.title: Confirm with the organizer
steps: Go to the organizer briefing: dates, rules, prizes and base camp options.
Name the project manager and two co-leads per squad, so no squad depends on one person.
Ask JMCC to offer Rally Paper to its delegations as volunteer hours.
Ask the organizer for their list of 24-hour venues (Concordia rooms close around 8 or 9pm; McGill allows overnight).

phases.title: Plan and start recruiting
steps: Write the project plan and the outreach tracker: clubs, student associations, JMCC delegations, the CASA newsletter.
Hand out flyers at the summer events (Flag Football in 2026).
Line up sponsors by mid-August: food for base camp, and logos in time for the shirts.

phases.title: Registration and content
steps: Put the Keela sign-up form live now, not the last week. Reuse the 2025 fields (squad, days, shifts, location, overnight, referrals, organization, newsletter) and add the delegation (for hours) and a media release.
Start the countdown posts and the recruitment video.
All-staff call: Rally Paper is a volunteering event for every staff member.

phases.title: Squads and shifts
steps: Put everyone in a squad and a shift: Saturday 8am to 2pm, 2 to 8pm and 8pm to midnight; Sunday midnight to 5am, 8am to noon and noon to 6pm.
Start WhatsApp fresh each year: one community, one chat per squad and an invite-only leaders chat. Never post answers in open chats.
Tabling on campus (Concordia, Vanier, Loyola) and a one-pager for club presidents.

phases.title: Lock the physical squad
steps: Lock the physical roster (gender-balanced) and send the organizer the waivers and the list.
Receive the Instagram account; give access to about 3 people and share the login through a password manager, never in a channel.
Prepare the pre-challenge booklet and post the intro video.
Leads meeting: the roster sheet (a Present column per squad) and the base camp plan.

phases.title: Results, hours and thanks
steps: Confirm the placing and the prize with the organizer, and record the money on the events calendar when it arrives.
Verify volunteer hours with JMCC (only hours actually done) and send them.
Thank everyone, post the result and return the Instagram account.
Hold the post-mortem and update this SOP.

dayof: Base camp opens before 8am Saturday; co-leads check people in against the roster.
Every 2 hours the booklet drops: split the work and submit before the deadline, every time.
The physical squad goes where the organizer sends it, 2 hours ahead, ready to get wet (the 2025 rules said to bring a swimsuit and towel).
Keep the online squad going overnight: the Saturday and Sunday co-leads hand over.
Food and drinks at base camp (from sponsors or the budget).
Every video on the lent account opens with the Rally Paper banner.
money: The prize is the fundraiser: 3rd place paid $1,000 in 2025.
Costs are small: about 100 printed flyers in 2026. Shirts and cars come from the organizer.
Food sponsors are worth asking: another team got about $200 to $300 of food.
lessons: Headcount decides the placing. In the organizer's words, "spirit was there, headcount was not."
Recruit early: in 2026 the sign-up form went live 12 days before the event. Put it up six weeks out.
JMCC delegations brought the most players; adding hundreds of people to WhatsApp brought few.
Two co-leads per squad, split Saturday and Sunday, so no squad fades overnight.
Share every piece of work between at least two people, so nothing stalls if someone steps away.
Test every email before it goes out.
Keep internal meetings few and short, at times people can make.
confirm: The official 2026 placing, the prize and when it arrives, and any MVP award.
The 2027 timing: the events calendar has Rally Paper 2027 in summer, but both editions ran in late September.

trainings.title: SOP: Gift Basket Drive
trainings.description: How we collect, pack and deliver holiday gift baskets to shelters and hospitals in December: partners, donations, the packing day and the deliveries.

body.intro: Every December we gather donated clothing, hygiene products, books and small joys, pack them into baskets on one big day, and deliver them to shelters and hospitals before Christmas. It is a drive for donated goods, not a cash fundraiser: the November events raise the money for it. Two editions so far, each bigger than the last.
glance: The packing day is the Sunday before Christmas; deliveries run until December 23
A church hall (2025: Union United Church, 3007 Rue Delisle)
Scattered (our co-founder of the drive), JMCC, Enactus Concordia and CEP
Ardene, Sportira, MiniBiblioPlus (300 books), Literacy Quebec and many individuals
3,000+ items in 446 baskets for six shelters, plus two hospitals (2025)
About 11 weeks (the first tasks go out in early October)
editions: 3,000+ items (2,000+ pieces of clothing, 200+ joy items, 100+ hygiene products) in 446 baskets: Chez Doris 46 (hygiene), Resilience 60, St Michael's 80, Logifem 80, Open Door 80 and Mission Bon Accueil 100, with the rest to the Montreal Children's (through the MUHC and Starlight foundations) and the Douglas. Jemeela coordinated the shelters, churches and itinerary (and wrote the 15-step template), Daniela led donor outreach, Steel handled partners, pickups and the venue, Natalia messaged volunteers, Soraya ran the newsletter, Ian and Patricia promoted it, and Scattered found the book and stationery donors.

Our first edition with Scattered, launched with a free talent show at Reggie's on December 20. Gifts went to the Douglas, the Royal Victoria, the Montreal Children's and an ICU: 1,500+ gifts, beating the goal.
roles: Shelters and hospitals, the venue, the itinerary and the delivery sheet
Companies and in-kind donors, the donation forms and pages
Partner organizations, donation pickups, storage and the venue
Recruiting through partners and the staff volunteering day, and reminders
The flyer, the newsletter, posts and the recap
One lead per packing line on the day

phases.title: Partners, venue and recipients
steps: Confirm the partners (Scattered, JMCC, Enactus) and open a WhatsApp group with each one.
Book the venue and secure storage for donations.
Contact shelters and hospitals now: ask how many baskets, what they need most and their delivery windows. Replies are slow (only two shelters had answered by mid-October 2025).
Set the target (2026: 4,000+ gifts).

phases.title: Donations
steps: Open the Keela forms for items, money and volunteers, and get the web donation page ready.
Ask companies and in-kind donors for clothing, books and hygiene products (in 2024 the Salvation Army gave clothing).
Tabling on campus with a sample basket.
Have the flyer, the tracker and the budget ready by mid-November.

phases.title: Volunteers and promotion
steps: Newsletter and posts.
Make the packing day a staff volunteering day, and ask JMCC and Enactus for volunteers early.
Tie the November fundraisers (the fashion show, the One Bag Challenge) to the drive.

phases.title: Plan the day
steps: A short planning meeting every week in December.
One packing day, not two.
Donation pickups in the week before.
Finish the delivery sheet: quantities, delivery windows and entry notes for each place.

phases.title: Thank and report
steps: Thank donors, partners and volunteers, and post the recap with the numbers.
Bring back everything we lent or used (tablecloths went missing in 2025).
Debrief and update this SOP.

dayof: 8am set-up. Public drop-off from 9am to 1pm at the venue.
Four packing lines: clothing (about 11 people), hygiene and food (8), joy items (7), and quality check, sealing and labeling (4).
Pizza lunch at noon.
Label every basket for its recipient from the delivery sheet.
Clean-up done by 5pm; deliveries start the same day.
Delivery notes that matter: text Chez Doris 5 minutes before arriving; use the loading dock at Mission Bon Accueil.
money: The 2025 budget template was $4,000: venue $1,500, gifts $1,000, ads $900 and supplies $600. Actual spending was not recorded: record it this year.
The drive collects goods, so the money comes from the November events and from donations.
lessons: Lock the partners and the venue earlier: partners can confirm late.
WhatsApp groups with partner organizations worked well.
Volunteers come from partners and the staff day; the public volunteer form brought 3 sign-ups in 2025.
One packing day works; two sessions did not.
Have the web donation pages ready by December.

trainings.title: SOP: Fundraisers run by student associations (JMCC, CASA)
trainings.description: How we work with JMCC and CASA when they run fundraising nights and weeks for Welfare Avenue: their part, our part, and collecting the money.

body.intro: Some of our best nights are run by student associations. JMCC (the JMSB competition committee) picks a charity each year and its VP Charity runs events for it. CASA JMSB chose us for its 5 Days for the Homeless week in March 2025 and again in 2026. They run the night; we advise, promote, show up, thank them, and make sure the money reaches us.
glance: A night at Reggie's and a bake sale in November (2024 and 2025), planned by the VP Charity (2026-27: Ryan Antosh)
5 Days for the Homeless in March, with a St. Patrick's party at Reggie's in 2025
JMCC about $2,000 (2024); CASA about $1,000 by cheque (2026)
Advise, promote, attend, thank, verify volunteer hours, collect the money
editions: A bake sale in early November and a Reggie's night on Thursday, November 21, run by VP Charity Charles Arsenault, with a donation link that counted toward JMCC's competition goal: about $2,000.

A fundraiser at Reggie's on Thursday, November 13 (5 to 8pm) with activities and merch, toward JMCC's $2,500 goal. Delegates also earned volunteer hours at the storage clean-up, Sunday servings and the Gift Basket Drive.

CASA JMSB's 5 Days for the Homeless: an awareness post, a food bank collection, a bake and merch sale, a free St. Patrick's party at Reggie's on Thursday, March 13 with shot sales going to us, sandwiches made and delivered on the Friday, and CASA serving with us on the Saturday. Gabriela coordinated for CASA and Jemeela pitched the themes.
5 Days for the Homeless again: about $1,000, paid by cheque.
roles: The relationship, the dates, the ask, collecting the money and the thank-yous
Posts and stories before and during the event, and the thank-you post
Come to the night, and to the serving the association joins
Track and verify JMCC delegates' hours

phases.title: Meet the new organizers
steps: Meet JMCC's VP Charity in September and CASA in January, and agree the dates early.
Share what worked (Reggie's nights, bake sales, merch) and what we can bring: a speaker, photos, a table.
Agree how the money reaches us (a donation link we control, an e-transfer or a cheque) and by when.
For JMCC, agree how delegates' volunteer hours are logged and verified.
Before booking Reggie's, check the rate: a 2022 note says it was free for nonprofits affiliated with Concordia.

steps: Share the event on our channels and in the newsletter; give them our logo and a short blurb.

trainings.title: SOP: Corporate volunteering days
trainings.description: How we host a company team for a cooking or serving day that the team also fundraises for: the pitch, the budget, the kitchen and the day.

body.intro: A company sends a team to cook or serve with us for a day, and the team raises money to cover the day and more. Fundraising sells and plans the day; Operations runs it. Since 2022 we have hosted GHD, RBC Van Horne, Oberoi Financial and Adaptavist, and Benevity has offered to send us more groups.
glance: A 4- or 8-hour cooking or serving day for 10 to 20 staff, with a fundraising goal
$2,000 or more per day. Send the budget first, so the company knows its goal.
Adaptavist, December 6, 2024: 15 volunteers, 250+ meals and $1,400+ raised (their blog)
editions: A pizza day at Union United Church, 10am to 4pm: 8 to 10 staff and 288 servings. Food cost about $470 to $540, plus $200 to $300 for the kitchen. Staff gave through Benevity.
A cooking day: 10 of their staff and 2 of ours, a 300-meal goal and a $2,000 target, with about $600 to $700 of food. Their blog reports 15 volunteers, 250+ meals and $1,400+ raised.
Summer events, most recently July 27, 2025 (one was lost to weather in 2024).
Engineers handed out meals, diapers, hygiene products, shoes and clothes (May 28, 2022 and May 31, 2025).
A volunteering day with the branch team.
roles: The pitch, the FAQ call, the budget and goal, the donation page, and the company relationship
The kitchen, the menu and food, the shelters receiving the meals, and running the day

phases.title: Pitch
steps: Send the pitch email and the pamphlet.
FAQ call: team size (10 to 20), a 4- or 8-hour day, possible dates and what they will do.

phases.title: Budget and goal
steps: Send the budget first, so the company knows its fundraising goal (aim for $2,000 or more).
Set up how they give: a donation page, or their workplace giving platform. Benevity took time to set up in 2025, so start now.

phases.title: Book and match
steps: Book the kitchen and the venue.
With Operations, choose the shelters that will receive the meals.
Keep Operations on the email thread from here on.

phases.title: Itinerary
steps: Send the itinerary a month ahead: arrival, safety and hygiene briefing, stations, lunch and deliveries.
Buy the food against the budget.

phases.title: Thank and report
steps: Thank the team with photos and the numbers: meals, people served, dollars raised.
Record the result, and invite them back next season.

dayof: Operations runs the kitchen; Fundraising hosts the company team.
Start with the safety and hygiene briefing, then the stations.
Photos for the company and for our channels.
Deliver the meals to the shelters on the itinerary.
money: Budget per day: food about $470 to $700, plus $200 to $300 for a kitchen when we rent one.
The company team fundraises the goal; send the budget before anything else.
lessons: Send the budget first: it sets the company's goal.
Workplace giving platforms take weeks to set up.
Companies go quiet between meetings: end every call with a next step and a date.
Fundraising owns the outreach and volunteer details; Operations owns the logistics.
confirm: What Adaptavist raised through Benevity in April 2025.

trainings.title: SOP: Serving at a partner's festival (Art4All)
trainings.description: How we serve meals and run a table at a partner's community festival, from Art4All with Scattered in June 2026.

body.intro: When a partner runs a community festival, we can bring food, a table and our volunteers. We did this at Scattered's Art4All festival on June 5, 2026: about 150 cold meals, then a table to meet people and recruit volunteers. It is not a fundraiser on its own, but it is how we meet new people and partners.
glance: Art4All with Scattered, Friday June 5, 2026, near 4 Rue Cloutier (Rosemont), 5 to 8pm
About 150 cold meals from 5 to 6:30pm, then a table and volunteer recruitment
Our tent, tables and tablecloths, the food and our signage
Only if Scattered brings it back in a format that fits (see the events calendar)
editions: Set-up at 4pm, about 150 cold meals, then the table. Amanda made 70+ sandwiches, Rami ran transport and photos, Ahmed brought the tent, Alexis made the poster, Shima owned the task and Steel led the team.

phases.title: Agree the format
steps: Agree with the partner: the date and times, what we serve, who the audience is, and the expected headcount so the food is sized right.
Confirm set-up time, space, power and water.

phases.title: Food and people
steps: Menu and quantities from the headcount, and who makes what.
Volunteers and transport; a WhatsApp group with the partner.

phases.title: Confirm
steps: Confirm the logistics in writing, and meet again if anything is unclear.
The poster and posts.

phases.title: Thank and debrief
steps: Thank the partner, debrief within two weeks and update this SOP.

dayof: Arrive an hour early to set up the tent, tables and the serving line.
Serve, then run the table: talk to people, recruit volunteers, collect emails.
Photos for the recap.
lessons: Get a headcount from the partner so the food is sized right.
Meet earlier and more often: the 2026 details were confirmed only about two weeks out.
A WhatsApp group with the partner worked.
Know the audience: Art4All serves the neurodivergent community, which is different from the people at our other events.

suggestions.why: Jun 25 Otter update states the team wants a roughly monthly cadence with Melvina driving, and open task calls to replicate the last event format toward monthly Toronto cadence.

suggestions.measure: Succession plan documented and two team members trained on core tasks by December 31, 2026

suggestions.measure: 20 active Toronto volunteers onboarded and participating in at least one event by December 31, 2026

Action items
6:41
Steel MacDonald: Find someone to handle bookkeeping/accounting for the organization because current staff are not strong in bookkeeping and the organization needs that role filled.
12:41
Accounting candidate: Explore and identify other avenues/ways to obtain more funding for the organization to increase annual revenue and mission impact.
24:28
Accounting candidate: Assess a proposal to rent a kitchen costing $150 every two weeks for operations, including determining if the expense fits the organization's budget and recommending approval or alternatives.
26:41
Steel MacDonald: Hold a small meeting including the accounting candidate, the organization's accountant, the Board Treasurer, and an executive to discuss how to manage accounting responsibilities and onboarding.
28:44
Steel MacDonald: Provide accounting and QuickBooks training resources and recommend free online courses or internal materials to support skill development for the accounting role (no paid training budget expected).
29:34
Steel MacDonald: If proceeding with the candidate, schedule start date; candidate indicated availability to start on Monday.
29:39
Steel MacDonald: Executive to discuss the candidate with the team and provide a hiring/next-step response, possibly by mid-week (Wednesday) following this meeting.
Summary

Steel MacDonald described the nonprofit's structure, limited budget, and need for a part-time accounting volunteer who can help maintain records and support fundraising. Rim Ammar explained relevant accounting education, brief prior internships, current freelance content role, recent arrival to Canada, flexible hours, and willingness to work unpaid to gain Canadian experience. Next steps: small onboarding meeting with Treasurer and external accountant, potential start as early as Monday, and a decision expected mid-week next week.

Organization structure and leadership 5:57
Steel MacDonald is the Executive Director and Founder; oversees marketing, fundraising, operations, development, programs and occasionally bookkeeping.
Organization started in 2020 and is small in scale with multiple volunteer leaders, including co-executive directors across cities.
Current challenge: lack of dedicated bookkeeping/accounting staff and searching for someone to support financial tasks.
Candidate education and accounting experience 6:56
Rim Ammar holds a master's in management, audit and control and completed three-month internships: one in an accounting firm and another in a public treasury establishment.
Rim currently works at Multimax creating content (magazines/books) and seeks this accounting placement to gain practical accounting experience.
Rim expressed an interest in progressing toward Canadian accounting practices and deepening accounting skills.
Relocation status and language/cultural fit 8:16
Rim arrived in Canada on April 22 (about two months prior) and is new to Canada and Montreal.
Rim values Montreal's Francophone environment and feels culturally comfortable; Rim can speak and understand some English and French.
Steel emphasized bilingual needs for the organization because team members are in Montreal and Toronto.
Availability and compensation expectations 10:01
Rim works as a freelancer ~15 hours/week with flexible scheduling and can accommodate the organization's ~10 hours/week request.
Rim is open to unpaid volunteer work to gain Canadian experience and deepen accounting skills; understands the nonprofit's limited budget.
Steel confirmed the role is flexible, part-time, and that many team members are volunteers; long-term commitment (even reduced hours) is preferred.
Nonprofit finances and priorities 12:02
Organization annual revenue is between $15,000 and $25,000, so finances are constrained and require frugality.
Key tasks: ensure numbers make sense, validate receipts and returns, prepare charitable donation receipts correctly, and analyze program vs overhead ratios.
Steel expects careful expense tracking and may request budget reviews to prioritize spending aligned with mission impact.
Role responsibilities, decision-making example and tools 17:47
Primary accounting tasks estimated at 2–3 hours/week (max ~10), including validating records and receipts; potential to help with fundraising or identifying revenue sources.
Steel presented a situational budgeting decision: evaluate paying $150 regularly for a shared kitchen vs volunteers cooking at home; Rim recommended checking budget fit and considering alternatives to save costs.
Tools and support: organization uses QuickBooks; Treasurer on the Board and an external accountant will provide guidance; an onboarding meeting with those stakeholders is planned.
Training, start date and next steps 27:19
Training: Steel can provide free internal training resources and recommend online courses; organization lacks funds to pay for external courses but will support learning.
Start date: Rim can begin as early as Monday; Steel will discuss with the team and provide a decision mid-week (possibly Wednesday).
Next steps: small meeting between Rim, the Treasurer, the external accountant and Steel to discuss account management and onboarding.

hub_knowledge.body:
Strategy deck prepared for Welfare Avenue by the Consulting Mandate Program (CMP, MCC), presented by Rian Khan, Aaron Itovitch, Albert Francis, Ahmad Saad, Jia Liu, Jad Chahine and Joud Arnaout. Full PDF is linked on the Important info page.

NATIONAL EXPANSION. Cities analyzed: Toronto (largest homeless population in Canada but saturated student club market), Ottawa (improving poverty rates, many clubs already address homelessness, collaboration potential), Vancouver (lower poverty rate, high housing costs, affordable housing advocacy focus), Calgary (strongest pick: 36 percent of residents cannot afford rent, 29 percent cannot afford healthy food, 25 percent cannot meet basic financial needs; only 2 poverty clubs at University of Calgary and none at SAIT; 58 percent of Calgarians volunteer yearly and 84 percent of seniors donate). Quebec City was ruled out. Sequence: Toronto expansion first (target universities UofT, TMU, York with named student org partners such as UofT Student Union Volunteer Network, Hart House Social Justice Committee, TMU Enactus, TMU Social Work Student Union, TMU Rotaract, YUSA Volunteer Hub, York Federation of Students), Calgary expansion planned in year 5 (2029/30).

TORONTO EXPANSION PHASES: 1 Research and development (identify key student organizations and contacts, contact outreach coordinators and faculty advisors, create recruitment materials, about 2 weeks). 2 Direct engagement and campus events (information sessions, collaborative events, campus volunteering and career fairs, launch a campus ambassador program, about 3 weeks). 3 Digital and social media (university social media and newsletters, university specific WhatsApp or Discord group, word of mouth and referral incentives, about 2 weeks). 4 Long term relationship (maintain communication with student leaders, end of term recognition and retention).

CHAPTER MODEL. Every chapter: Chapter President plus five VPs (Finance, Marketing, Events, Admin, External) plus 1 to 2 brand ambassadors; hire directors to aid functions; national VPs share reports and workflows. Chapter onboarding runs about 9 months: months 1-2 candidate identification (internal HQ search, mass message, online search, direct outreach, screening), months 3-4 chapter setup (university club registration, VP recruitment, bank account), months 5-9 training and support (operations training, sample events, ongoing support). Chapters sign a Chapter Affiliation Agreement covering use of the WA name and branding, financial accountability with quarterly financial reports, and consequences for non compliance (pause activities, revoke affiliation). Chapters need a constitution per their student union, must follow federal and provincial charity law, financial policies (budgeting, expense approvals, reporting; universities may audit), and data privacy rules. National oversight: Executive Director (vision, final say on legal and branding), National Programs Lead (coordinates chapters), Communications and Outreach Lead (approves messaging templates, social guidelines), Fundraising and Finance Lead (grants, national donors, legal filings).

COMMUNICATION PROTOCOLS. Day to day: Slack channels by function, daily check ins for task tracking, etiquette of clear subject lines, tagged mentions, responses within 24 hours. Meetings: weekly President with VPs (progress, challenges, action items), monthly Chapter Presidents with national C suite (strategic goals, fundraising and finance, governance). Crisis: immediate escalation via Slack and phone, incident documented in a standardized report within 24 hours, HQ assists with public statements.

RECRUITMENT AND LEADERSHIP. Philosophies: recruitment is an active continuous process; lean teams work better; screen for integrity, intelligence and energy (Buffett test); referrals outweigh experience; second in commands can be taught. Org structure moves from 4 levels, 10 divisions, 45 positions to 3 levels, 5 divisions, 26 positions. Leadership ladder: Board of Directors (supporting cast to the C suite, implement vision), C suite (report to the CEO, cultivate next generation of leaders), Club President (starts a new club, regular contact with C suite), Club VP (supports president, develops next year team), Brand Ambassador (networks and spreads the mission on campus). Recruit profiles: presidents score highest on quick learning, self starting, referrals and vision; VPs on self starting and energy; ambassadors on energy and integrity. Key implication: recruit critical thinkers for top roles, let high energy people be second in command, keep teams lean.

FIVE YEAR PLAN, four pillars: Organizational Development, Infrastructure and Operations, Community Growth, Fundraising and Sustainability. Year 1: hire fundraising and sponsorship manager and CFO, secure Montreal storage, acquire a van, integrate Keela and improve the website, partner with restaurants and grocery stores, implement the volunteer recruitment system. Year 2: continue restaurant and grocery partnerships, volunteer recruitment program, monthly outreach events, reorganize the org chart, hire CLO, promote team leaders, acquire Toronto storage and van. Year 3: leadership growth, corporate volunteer program launch, improve internal communications, expand Keela usage. Year 4: appoint regional directors for new cities, establish a national advisory board, develop the long term sustainability model. Year 5 (2029/30): sustainability strategy, multi city logistics upgrades, Calgary expansion. Toronto budget grows from about 2,860 dollars in year 1 to 6,820 in year 5 (ambassador incentives, 3 events per year, marketing with the Google Ad Grant covering digital, volunteer training, TTC fare subsidies, 5 to 10 percent contingency).

REVENUE TARGETS. Local business sponsorships: about 5,000 dollars annually (small and mid sized businesses commonly give around that to local nonprofits). Canada Summer Jobs (CSJ): wage subsidies up to 100 percent of provincial minimum wage for youth 15 to 30; target two summer positions per year, roughly 15,000 dollars. Alternative streams considered: joint event nights with student associations (raffles, venues, donations; competitive to secure) and checkout charity campaigns (broad awareness, passive revenue, weaker audience fit under inflation).

SEO AND CONTENT. Current standing: domain rating 17 of 100, 2,200 backlinks but only 22 dofollow, 115 linking sites (13 dofollow). Top keywords: volunteer area, volunteering, non profit organizations, community service, volunteer opportunities. Content plan, three post types: High Authority posts (advice on accessing aid, e.g. How To Access Financial Aid in Montreal, Canadian Government Programs), Feel Good posts (accomplishments and stories, e.g. Interview with Steel MacDonald, event recaps), Community posts (WA in lists of local initiatives, e.g. Fighting Food Insecurity in Montreal, How Volunteering Can Change Lives). Outstanding: blog debut and a SemRush free trial deep dive.

SPONSORSHIP ACQUISITION PROCESS. Build the package: collect WA history highlights, identify most successful events, plan future events with budget bounds and needed support, define sponsorship tiers matching WA colors and vision. Outreach: 1 set up the meeting (reach out with the sponsor goal, schedule, keep a paper trail in the Excel tracker), 2 prepare (internal goals per sponsor, tailor the package, confirm and remind, send the package by mail), 3 during the meeting (introduce WA, walk the package, invite questions), 4 follow up (check for concerns or a decision, schedule next meetings). CasaCares contacts: VP Events Arko Tamjid, VP External Lea Conde; RBC branch contact Raymond for partnership next steps.

request_types.label: Social media post request
request_types.description: Ask the marketing team to create and publish a social media post. Requests follow the standard brief: purpose, target audience, call to action, assets, and preferred platform.

request_types.label: Email request
request_types.description: Ask the marketing team to draft and send an email or newsletter. Provide the objective, intended audience, key messages, and deadlines: the team drafts, seeks approval, and sends.

request_types.label: Design request
request_types.description: Ask the marketing design team to produce a branded visual asset such as a banner, flyer, tent, or report layout. Include context, specs or supplier links, and the brand direction to apply.

request_types.label: Reimbursement request
request_types.description: Request approval and repayment for a purchase made on behalf of Welfare Avenue. List the items and prices, wait for approval from Finance or the Executive Director, then upload the photo receipt.

request_types.label: Position recruitment request
request_types.description: Ask HR to recruit a new position. Provide the role title, a link to the job description, and the number of interview stages needed: HR defines the role, posts the job, and runs interviews.

request_types.label: New member onboarding
request_types.description: Ask HR to onboard a new team member following the Onboarding SOP. HR tracks the member from recruitment through 30, 60, and 90 day check-ins to full membership.

request_types.label: Purchase order request
request_types.description: Request approval to spend organizational money before buying. Finance approves, then you purchase and file the receipt through a reimbursement if you fronted it.

request_types.label: Event supplies request
request_types.description: Ask operations to source or bring supplies for a serving event: containers, gloves, tables, signage, water.

request_types.label: Volunteer support request
request_types.description: Ask the volunteering team for extra hands: more cooks, drivers, servers or a photographer for a specific event.

request_types.label: Tool or account access request
request_types.description: Request access to a Welfare Avenue tool or account: email, ClickUp, Canva, the dashboard, Quo, drive folders.

request_types.label: Event photo and video coverage
request_types.description: Ask marketing for a photographer, videographer or social coverage at an event. Give the event, date, location, and what content is needed (photos, reels, testimonials). Marketing books the person and files the media afterwards.

request_types.label: Printing request
request_types.description: Ask marketing to get something physically printed: shirts, flyers, banners, signage, cards. Include quantities, sizes, the design or a design request, the deadline, and where it needs to be delivered.

request_types.label: Transportation request
request_types.description: Ask operations for a vehicle, driver or pickup and delivery help: moving coolers, equipment, donations or supplies. Give what is being moved, from where to where, the date, and any lifting help needed. Route to Ops Toronto when it concerns Toronto.

request_types.label: Media release and consent
request_types.description: Ask leadership to draft, update or apply consent and media release language: photo and video release clauses on volunteer or event forms, and handling for people who decline to be filmed. Legal and governance reviews the wording.

request_types.label: Grant information request
request_types.description: Ask the grants team for information or documents needed for a grant application or report, or flag a grant opportunity: eligibility details, budgets, letters, statistics about our programs. Include the deadline and the funder.

content_drafts.title: Sponsor pitch: Montreal grocery chain Sunday kitchen partnership
content_drafts.body_md:
I'm writing on behalf of Welfare Avenue, a youth led nonprofit building a scalable model for social reintegration in Montreal and Toronto.

Every Sunday, we run a community kitchen that serves as the first step in restoring dignity and trust for people experiencing precarity. The meal is the conduit. It creates the consistent, judgment free environment where people can access the broader safety net: housing support, mental health referrals, employment pathways.

We're inviting [confirm: grocery chain name] to sponsor ingredients on a monthly basis.

Your investment would directly support our Sunday operations while offering high visibility CSR impact. We're piloting on-site donation collection, and a partnership with a trusted local grocer strengthens both the consistency of our service and the credibility of the model we're scaling across both cities.

This is not about handing out food. It's about using shared meals as the bridge to holistic reintegration, and doing it with the discipline and structure of a professional organization.

I'd welcome the chance to discuss what a partnership could look like, including recognition opportunities and reporting on impact.

Are you available for a brief call in the next two weeks?

Best regards,

Steel MacDonald  
Co-Executive Director  
Welfare Avenue

content_drafts.title: Sponsor one-pager: Flag Football fundraiser August 2026
content_drafts.body_md:
## Welfare Avenue Flag Football Tournament

**August 2026 | Montreal**

Welfare Avenue is hosting a charity flag football tournament this August to expand our capacity to build trust and restore dignity through shared meals and social reintegration services in Montreal and Toronto.

This is an opportunity to align your brand with a youth-led professional organization that delivers measurable impact in one of Canada's fastest-growing social service ecosystems.

## Why Flag Football

A high-visibility community event that brings together corporate teams, university groups, and community supporters in a day of sport, connection, and solidarity.

All proceeds fund our scalable meal and reintegration model: food as the conduit, trust as the foundation, dignity and social reintegration as the goal.

## Confirmed Partners

Dose Juices has confirmed as a beverage partner.

Enactus McGill and Enactus Concordia are secured as university partners, bringing student energy and reach across Montreal campuses.

## Sponsorship Benefits

- Brand visibility at a high-energy community event attended by youth leaders, corporate teams, and community organizations
- Logo placement on event materials, social media, and day-of signage
- Alignment with a professional nonprofit recognized for innovation, discipline, and impact
- Direct CSR storytelling: your investment funds meals, builds trust, and supports pathways to housing, employment, and health services

[confirm: sponsorship tiers and pricing]

## About Welfare Avenue

Welfare Avenue is a youth-led nonprofit operating in Montreal and Toronto.

We use shared meals as the starting point for dignity, trust, and social reintegration. Food is the conduit; the meal builds trust; our work connects people to housing, employment, health, and legal services through a collaborative ecosystem of specialized partners.

We are a bridge, not a silo. We build the initial relationship, then refer to the right agency at the right time.

Service is solidarity, not charity.

## Next Steps

We would welcome the opportunity to discuss sponsorship tiers and how your organization can be part of this event.

[confirm: contact name and email for sponsor inquiries]

For more information, visit [confirm: website] or reach out directly.

onboarding_template.name: Policies
onboarding_template.description:
Please read Welfare Avenue's organizational policies: the [full version](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_M0fdr3P71Y95ptj-6toA6phRYHaKCsG/edit) or the [summarized version](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Sg62q5H4KktrYTp0tGneto4ruouwgLbU5lej4gkMo5E/edit). It is crucial that everyone takes the time to review them and surfaces any questions. Leave this in progress until you have read it in full.

The policies also live in the shared [Org Files > HR folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Q0YRW5TroUNSI411lYaNbWIEvz7BvKvb) along with the [90 day evaluation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TXKgL8V-JGvRneKa6BGuRUrjeGJ_pYfs/edit). Ask questions in your onboarding channel, or comment on the doc and tag someone.

**To complete the task:** after reading the policies, ask HR to send you the document to sign on DocuSign.

onboarding_template.name: Intros
onboarding_template.description:
**Introduce yourself in your team's channel:** your name and role, where you are located, and a fun fact or a little interest. Do this before your first meeting with your department.

**Introduce yourself in the General chat:** your name and role, plus a quick sentence on what you are looking forward to. Do this within your first four days.

Articles to read: [Montreal Guardian on Welfare Avenue](https://montrealguardian.com/montreal-charity-welfare-avenue/), [The Link on the gentrification of thrifting](https://thelinknewspaper.ca/article/the-gentrification-of-thrifting), [CBC on Montreal homelessness and Welfare Avenue](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/montreal-homeless-welfare-avenue-1.6470047).

**To complete the task:** tell us what stuck with you or what you learned about us in your onboarding channel. A small message will do.

onboarding_template.name: Slack
onboarding_template.description: Get set up on Slack, our main communication tool. Complete the items below.

onboarding_template.name: ClickUp beginner guide
onboarding_template.description: Complete the [ClickUp Beginners Course, about 30 minutes](https://university.clickup.com/path/clickup-for-beginners). Once completed, send a message in your onboarding channel answering: what was most useful, and how do you see yourself using ClickUp at Welfare Avenue? Then work through the mini topics below.

onboarding_template.name: Mandatory volunteering
onboarding_template.description:

**To complete the task:** tell your manager the date you will be volunteering.

onboarding_template.name: Self-assessment
onboarding_template.description:
Write a short self-assessment on your first three weeks: what went well and what you like so far; what challenges you faced; what skills or areas you want to learn more about; where you see yourself contributing more. Keep it light, this is only to get your feedback.

**To complete the task:** send your answers in your onboarding channel or to your HR rep and manager.

onboarding_template.name: Pick up a training path
onboarding_template.description: Pick one training path and work through it: browse them on the Training tab here in the Hub, or in the [ClickUp Training Paths list](https://app.clickup.com/9017695379/v/li/901711441932). Your team lead can help you choose the right one for your role.

onboarding_template.name: Performance and discipline tracking
onboarding_template.description:
[Performance and discipline tracking](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PHhf41ChaLOZu4ybsWyEpXrsKIQLDDlCN-_kfq7sH5c/edit) and [watch the HR walkthrough](https://www.loom.com/share/4a330c1733b8473a8bf5252c0ce3f990).

**Mini task:** after reading the policies, ask your HR representative to send the policy document to sign in your onboarding channel.

onboarding_template.name: Set up
onboarding_template.description: Watch these videos for a better understanding of Slack and set up your profile: [Part 1](https://www.loom.com/share/1edbc0c25e1b484db405dfabd291dc1d) and [Part 2](https://www.loom.com/share/7dbc52dabfcc484181ce6f8ddc1f111d). Comment "done" under the Part 2 video when you finish it.

onboarding_template.name: Training and development channel
onboarding_template.description: [Watch the video](https://www.loom.com/share/81c73a6731474896afda755450b06723) and the [updated May 2025 rundown](https://www.loom.com/share/a8c8aa9d8f6842a998ab674dffc5d771). Ask your manager which additional trainings you should do. Once done, add your name to the training and say which ones you completed in your onboarding channel.

onboarding_template.name: Optimizing and organizing your Slack

onboarding_template.description: Book a 15 minute meeting with the Executive Director. Send a Google Calendar invite (see Setting up a meeting, Week 1) and post in your onboarding channel once it is booked.

onboarding_template.name: Assigning comments
onboarding_template.description:
1. Find the comment section of this task on the right.
2. Write "Hi @manager name, this is a test to assign comments in ClickUp."

Remember: you can see all comments others have assigned to you on your ClickUp home page.

onboarding_template.name: Hierarchy in ClickUp
onboarding_template.description:
**Workspace.** Your Workspace is the top level. Welfare Avenue is a workspace. Each ClickUp Workspace is entirely separate, so information cannot be viewed or transferred between them.

**Spaces.** Spaces divide the Workspace into big chunks, each customisable. Example: Organization goals, Operations, Marketing, Outreach and Accounting are all Spaces (departments).

**Folders and lists.** Folders group Lists, and Lists contain tasks. Lists separate different work processes: in Marketing, one list holds posts, one digital campaigns, one the website, one general tasks. Every task must live in a List.

**Tasks.** Tasks take the features of their Space and the workflow of their List. You can move a task at any time; workflow settings (statuses, custom fields) change at the Space, Folder or List level.

**Assigned comments** act as action items that notify the assigned person and stay visible until resolved. **Subtasks** carry the same traits as their parent task. **Checklists** are simple nested to-do lists (done or not done).

To complete this task: comment "@your manager, hey I am understanding ClickUp a bit better" and assign the comment to your manager.

onboarding_template.name: The slash function
onboarding_template.description:
The slash function is super powerful. Try it in any description or comment: type "/" and all the options pop up.

1. Play around with it and see how many functions you can find.
2. Comment a green button that directs anyone who clicks it to Welfare Avenue's website.
3. Use the slash function in the description to mention any doc within ClickUp.
4. Lastly, use the slash function to close this task.

Research & Data Analyst (Volunteer) - Job Description
wa_drive_docs.text_content:
Research & Data Analyst (Volunteer)
Welfare Avenue

Role overview
Supports the program development team with research and data.

Key responsibilities
- Design and run beneficiary surveys twice a year
- Maintain the beneficiary feedback dashboard and share monthly findings
- Track programme KPIs and flag gaps to the program development lead
- Support grant reports with clean data and short summaries
- Document research methods so the next volunteer can pick them up

Requirements
- Comfortable with spreadsheets
